---
title: Lazy Operations
---

A patch whose data are not read yet holds a [`LazyArray`](`dascore.lazy.array.LazyArray`), which [`Spool.set_backend`](`dascore.core.spool.Spool.set_backend`) gives it under the name `"lazy"`: a [`Recipe`](`dascore.lazy.recipe.Recipe`), which says which stored samples fill which box of the array, and a chain of the operations run on it since. An operation on such a patch computes nothing. Its kernel appends the processor and its plan to the chain, and [`Patch.load`](`dascore.Patch.load`) runs the chain: on the whole array when that is small, and a chunk at a time when it is not. The rules below are what let the work be split without changing any result. The code cells execute against the real machinery, so this note fails the doc build if it drifts from the implementation.

```{python}
import numpy as np

import dascore as dc
from dascore.core.source import ArraySource
from dascore.lazy.recipe import Recipe

recipe = Recipe.from_source(ArraySource.full((4, 3), -2.0))
coords = {"distance": np.arange(4), "time": np.arange(3)}
lazy = dc.Patch(data=recipe, coords=coords, dims=("distance", "time"))

out = lazy.abs().update_attrs(station="here").angle()
print(type(out.data).__name__, len(out.data.chain))
```

## The rules a lazy operation keeps

**Chunk size is an implementation detail.** The result is the same, within floating-point precision, whether it was computed whole or a chunk at a time, and it has the same `data_id`. An operation states what a chunk of its output needs of its input by returning a [chunk contract](`dascore.lazy.contract`) from [`chunk_contract`](`dascore.core.processor.PatchProcessor.chunk_contract`), given the input's dtype and its plan. The contracts are listed [below](#the-contracts). A contract is decided from the dtype and the plan, never from the values: an operation whose no-op depends on the values, such as `fillna`, cannot state one.

**Metadata is never lazy.** A lazy patch always has concrete coords, attrs, shape and dtype. They come from `get_metadata`, which runs when the operation is called and knows nothing of chunks, so it must state the dtype the kernel returns as well as the shape. [`load`](`dascore.lazy.array.LazyArray.load`) checks each step's result against what its metadata stated, and refuses a mismatch naming the processor. An operation whose metadata depends on the data cannot be lazy.

```{python}
loaded = out.load()
assert loaded.dtype == out.dtype and loaded.shape == out.shape
```

**The lazy backend never falls back unasked.** An operation with no contract raises [`LazyOperationError`](`dascore.exceptions.LazyOperationError`) before anything is read, where another backend would convert to NumPy, unless the `numpy_fallback` setting allows the read; see [Backends](#backends). Arithmetic and NumPy functions on the patch, whichever operand is lazy, `rolling`, stacking a spool, and the waterfall and specplot figures raise it whatever the setting. A patch's repr describes lazy data without reading them. Unless the setting allows more, the data are read in these places only:

- `Patch.load` (and `Spool.load`, which calls it), `np.asarray(patch)`, writing the patch to a file, and `Patch.set_backend` naming a backend in memory, or a spool set to one handing out a lazy patch it holds, where the caller asks for the values;
- `Patch.equals` (and `==`), which compares them.

Everything else refuses. A spool with no lazy backend reads its files as it always has: those data were never lazy.

```{python}
from dascore.exceptions import LazyOperationError

try:
    lazy.detrend("time")
except LazyOperationError as error:
    print(error)
```

**Each step has its own identity.** A step's `data_id` is the one [`PatchProcessor`](`dascore.core.processor.PatchProcessor`) records for an eager patch: derived from the operation's id and the previous patch's `data_id`. The node records the id the patch was given at that step, so every lazy step has the eager step's id, and an eager no-op (an `Unchanged` contract) hands back the patch itself, id and all. A metadata-only operation changes the patch's id and leaves the lazy array as it was; the patch's `attrs.data_id` is what names the patch.

```{python}
eager = lazy.load().abs().update_attrs(station="here").angle()
assert loaded.attrs.data_id == eager.attrs.data_id == out.attrs.data_id
assert lazy.real() is lazy  # real data: nothing to do, as eagerly
```

## The contracts

A chunk is a box of the array: one slice for each axis. A contract says which box of its input a box of its output is computed from, and nothing else about chunks; no operation chooses a chunk size or loops over chunks.

| Contract | A box of the output needs | Stated by |
|---|---|---|
| `Pointwise` | the same box of the input | `abs`, `real`, `imag`, `angle`, `conj` |
| `Halo` | the same box and a fixed number of samples around it, stopping at the ends of the array | `median_filter`, `gaussian_filter`, and `savgol_filter` with an edge mode other than its default; `pass_filter` and `notch_filter` called on a [`Patch.impulse_window`](`dascore.Patch.impulse_window`), by the reach their response to an impulse measures |
| `WholeAxis` | the whole of some axes, and the same place along the others | `pass_filter`; the three above when their edge mode wraps; `savgol_filter` in its default mode, which fits a polynomial to each end of what it is given |
| `Window` | the same box moved by where a selection starts | `select` with ranges |
| `Tiles` | the tiles which overlap the box, each whole; along the other axes, what the operation in the window states | a patch operation called on a [`Patch.window`](`dascore.Patch.window`) |
| `Unchanged` | nothing: the kernel hands its input back | `real` and `conj` of real data, a `select` which keeps everything |

The filters state a contract for `float32` and `float64` data only, the dtypes their kernels return as given, and `gaussian_filter` states none when its edge mode is given axis by axis. A query which does not resolve to one range for each dimension is no window and is refused: a `select` by an array of values or a mask, and what `unselect` and `order` build.

A patch operation called on a window is computed a tile at a time and blended, so it states `Tiles` whatever the operation is. The tiles are placed by the array and not by the box: a box is grown out to the edges of the tiles which overlap it, each of those is computed whole, and the box is cut from the blend. A windowed axis can therefore be cut even where the operation alone needs it whole, and `window(time=10).detrend("time")` runs on a lazy patch where `detrend("time")` is refused. Along an axis which is not windowed the box needs what the operation's own contract says, and the whole axis where it states none. Where the operation keeps every n-th sample of a windowed axis, as `fbe` with a `step` does, the result is shorter than what it is computed from: a box counts samples of the result, the tiles which overlap it are found in those samples, and those tiles are read from the input. The lazy patch states its dtype by running the operation's kernel once on a window of zeros, since an operation with no contract has never had to state what its kernel returns. A reduction in a window and a function given to `apply` state no contract yet, so both are refused on a lazy patch.

A `Halo` kernel sees the true ends of the array in the chunks which hold them, so it treats them as it does eagerly, and what it makes of a cut end is trimmed off. A halo never reaches past an earlier selection: to a filter after a `select`, the window's ends are the array's.

## How a chain runs

[`dascore.lazy.execute`](`dascore.lazy.execute`) does the work in three separate steps.

1. **Cut the result into boxes.** If no array the result needs is larger than the `lazy_block_size` setting, there is one box. There is also one box when no step computes anything, since reading in pieces would only open each file again. Otherwise the box is halved along the first axis worth cutting until they fit. An axis an operation needs whole is not worth cutting, and nor is one already short beside its halo, so the block size is aimed for rather than promised.
2. **Work out what each box reads.** Each step's contract is asked, last to first, which box of its input it needs. Nothing is read to answer, so every read is known before the first one happens.
3. **Read and compute each box.** The recipe reads only the box needed, and each step's kernel for the array's library runs on it, first to last: each run of steps with a kernel for the library is handed to the backend's `run_chain`, which a backend may compile (see [Compiling a chain](#compiling-a-chain)).

A selection therefore narrows what is read wherever it sits in the chain.

```{python}
from dascore.lazy.execute import chunk_boxes, read_schedule

recipe = Recipe.from_source(ArraySource.full((8, 1_000), 1.0))
coords = {"distance": np.arange(8), "time": np.arange(1_000)}
big = dc.Patch(data=recipe, coords=coords, dims=("distance", "time"))

chain = big.median_filter(time=5, samples=True).select(time=(100, 200), samples=True)
boxes = chunk_boxes(chain.data)
print(boxes, read_schedule(chain.data, boxes))
```

The whole result is still put together in memory; writing each box out as it is made is a later change, and [Windowed and Lazy Processing](windowed_processing.qmd) is the plan for it and for what else is to come. Until then:

- No data or computed result is kept between loads. Each piece a spool cuts from a lazy patch runs the chain for itself, so a piece cut along an axis a step needs whole reads and computes that whole axis again. A backend which compiles may keep what it compiled (see [Compiling a chain](#compiling-a-chain)), which is code, not data.
- A kernel is not run until the chain is, so an argument its kernel refuses, such as an edge mode scipy does not know, is refused at `load` rather than at the call.
- A step which recorded no contract, as a kernel registered for the lazy backend may leave, is given all of its input.

## Backends

A backend says how a spool makes the array each of its patches holds. [`Spool.set_backend`](`dascore.core.spool.Spool.set_backend`) takes an [`ArrayBackend`](`dascore.backends.ArrayBackend`), whose options are fields of the instance, or the name of a registered one, which is that backend with its default options. `"numpy"` holds the data in memory, and another package can register a backend for its own array library (see [A backend from another package](#a-backend-from-another-package)). `"lazy"`, or its alias `"LazyArray"`, reads nothing until the data are asked for, and in brackets names the backend each box is computed on: `"lazy"` is `"lazy[numpy]"`. A spool with no backend set hands out whatever its files' readers return.

```{python}
from dascore.utils.downloader import fetch

spool = dc.spool(fetch("example_dasdae_event_1.h5")).set_backend("lazy")
waiting = spool[0].abs()
print(type(waiting.data).__name__, type(waiting.load().data).__name__)
```

- **A patch** says which backend it is of with `patch.backend`, which is `None` when it was given none, and `patch.set_backend` puts it on one: the patch is what a spool holding it, set to that backend, would hand out. A patch of a backend holds that backend's arrays, so `patch.new(data=array)` makes other data its backend's, where a patch of no backend holds whatever it is given. A patch in memory set to a lazy backend stays in memory, on the backend the lazy one computes on, since a lazy patch is a promise to read and one made in memory has nothing to read.
- **A backend states a name and an array type.** The `name` is any name in lower case: what a string calls the backend, what its kernels are registered under, and what a package names its `dascore.kernels` entry point, so DASCore imports the backend the first time the name is asked for. The `array_type` is the class of its arrays, or a string of where the class is such as `"array_api_strict._array_object.Array"`. Two backends may make the same arrays under different names: a `"numba"` backend subclassing `NumpyBackend` hands out NumPy arrays, and an operation on them runs the kernel registered for `"numba"`. An operation with none runs what the array would anyway, with nothing said, since nothing is converted.
- **Kinds of array are not mixed.** Two patches of different array libraries are not added, joined or merged, since neither is put on the other's library; a lazy patch counts as what it loads to, and a NumPy patch of no backend is still taken in by another library in arithmetic. Patches of one kind combine, and the result is of the first one's backend.
- **An option is a field of the backend.** An [`ArrayAPIBackend`](`dascore.backends.ArrayAPIBackend`) takes a `device`: `LazyBackend(compute=Strict(device=device))`, with `Strict` the backend [below](#a-backend-from-another-package), computes each box on that device, where `"lazy[strict]"` leaves the library to choose. Two backends are equal when their options are.
- **An array of no array library is NumPy's.** An array-like which keeps its values some other way, compressed say, is handed out as it is under no backend, `"numpy"` or `"lazy"`; only another library, which was asked for by name, has it converted.
- **Another library registers a backend** as [shown below](#a-backend-from-another-package). A backend with an array type of its own subclasses [`ArrayBackend`](`dascore.backends.ArrayBackend`) and says in `from_array` how one is made from an array in memory. A backend which reads for itself overrides `from_recipe`; one which makes its arrays from a stored window as it is, with no recipe, overrides `from_source`, which a read hands each window it selected.
- **A spool** hands out each patch on its backend: read lazily where a read can be, which is a selection of neighbouring samples from a format which names its stored arrays. A spool made from it, as by `select` or `sort`, keeps the backend. Lazy reading is in force only while the spool reads a patch: a `dc.read` the caller makes while iterating it fills memory as usual. Spools added together are on the first backend any of them was set to, so a spool with none takes the other's, and their backends must make arrays of one kind.
- **A merge stays lazy.** Under a lazy backend `spool.chunk(time=None)[0]` is one lazy patch whose recipe names a window of each file, built from the index with no file opened. A selection made before `load` reads only the files it touches. The files are checked against the index when the patch is made; one rewritten between then and `load` is refused only if it no longer holds an array of the shape and dtype its row states.
- **Merging and concatenating join data where they are.** Lazy patches with nothing pending and one dtype, which are windows of what is stored, are joined by their recipes and stay lazy, whether a spool merges files the index describes or members it reads as patches, or concatenates them along a dimension they have. Patches in memory on one array library are joined by that library's own `concat`, so dask data, or data on any other array library, are never taken through NumPy for it.
- **Each box is computed on the library named**, by the kernel each step has for that library. A step with none has each box converted through NumPy.

One setting, `numpy_fallback`, decides a conversion through NumPy and a read of lazy data which was not asked for: `"raise"` refuses it, `"warn"` converts with a `NumpyFallbackWarning`, and `"ignore"` converts silently. Left unset it is `"raise"` for lazy data and `"warn"` for any other. It decides an operation with no kernel for an array library, an operation with no contract on a lazy patch (which reads the data into memory), a read which cannot be lazy (a selection of samples which are not next to each other, or a format which names no stored array or reads by a method of its own), a fill of a gap between files, and a merge or concatenation which cannot stay lazy: lazy patches with operations pending or of different dtypes, a mix of lazy patches and patches in memory, members in different data units, a new dimension for lazy patches, or members whose dtypes promote differently a member at a time than all at once. Patches of different array libraries are not joined at all, whatever the setting. A patch a spool already holds in memory is not read, so it is not made lazy. Nothing is converted or read unasked without the setting having allowed it, and a step already pending is asked again when a spool hands its patch out on another library. Arithmetic and NumPy functions on a lazy patch, `rolling`, the waterfall and specplot figures, and stacking a spool of lazy patches are refused whatever it says. `Spool.load` was asked to read everything, so it reads what could not have been lazy without asking the setting, onto the library a lazy backend computes on.

### A backend from another package

DASCore ships the `"numpy"` and `"lazy"` backends and no backend for any other array library. A package adds one in a module which defines the backend and registers its kernels, and names that module in an entry point.

- **The backend** subclasses [`ArrayAPIBackend`](`dascore.backends.ArrayAPIBackend`), and states `module` where the library's `asarray` is not in the top-level package of its array type.
- **Its kernels** are registered under its name with [`register_kernel`](`dascore.core.processor.register_kernel`). An operation with none runs the kernel registered under the library's own name, as [`backend_name`](`dascore.utils.array_api.backend_name`) spells it, or else its array-API kernel, and converts through NumPy only when it has neither, as `numpy_fallback` says.
- **The entry point**, in the `dascore.kernels` group and named after the backend, is loaded the first time a string names the backend, `"lazy[<name>]"` included, so a user need not import the package.

The module, say `strict_kernels/backend.py`, run here as a cell, and a patch put on its backend:

```{python}
import array_api_strict

from dascore.backends import ArrayAPIBackend
from dascore.core.processor import register_kernel
from dascore.proc.basic import Abs


class Strict(ArrayAPIBackend):
    """Arrays of array_api_strict."""

    name = "strict"
    array_type = "array_api_strict._array_object.Array"


@register_kernel(Abs, "strict")
def _abs(processor, data):
    """Return the absolute values on array_api_strict."""
    return array_api_strict.abs(data)


patch = dc.get_example_patch().set_backend("strict")
print(patch.backend, type(patch.abs().data).__module__)
```

The entry point, in the package's `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[project.entry-points."dascore.kernels"]
strict = "strict_kernels.backend"
```

### Compiling a chain

A box is computed by [`ArrayBackend.run_chain`](`dascore.backends.ArrayBackend.run_chain`), handed a run of the chain's steps and the box's data. By default it runs each step's kernel in turn, holding each result as one of the backend's arrays. A backend which compiles overrides it, and everything a compiled chain needs is in the [`Step`](`dascore.lazy.execute.Step`)s it is handed, so it never reaches into DASCore.

- **A step** holds the operation, its kernel for the backend, its plan, its contract, the box of input it is given and the box of output it makes, and the shape and dtype its metadata stated. `step.run(data)` runs it, checks the result against what was stated, and cuts it to its box; the check reads only shapes and dtypes, which are known while a chain is traced.
- **The plan is split in two.** `step.arrays` holds every array in it, nested ones too, and `step.static` the rest. A compiled chain is handed the arrays as arguments, so another patch whose coefficients have the same shapes runs what was compiled. It holds the rest fixed, so a new window length compiles again, as it must since shapes change. A processor lists in `plan_arrays` the entries to hand over as arrays though they are not, such as a float whose new values should not mean compiling again.
- **A key** says what a compiled chain is specialized to, and boxes of one shape cut alike along a patch share one; [`Step.key`](`dascore.lazy.execute.Step.key`) says what it holds. A backend adds the shape and dtype of the data it is handed, as the example below does. A tiled step, as `Patch.window` makes, is keyed by how the box is cut from its tiles and where the first sits among the tiles between two which do not overlap, and the boxes are cut a whole number of such runs long, so a long windowed load compiles for its two ends and its middle.
- **Sections.** A step with no kernel for the library goes through NumPy and is not handed to `run_chain`: the chain is run up to it and on from it, and the step is run between, so a backend only sees steps it has kernels for.
- **Caching is the backend's.** What it keeps, for how long, and whether on disk, are options of the backend, as its fields; none is a DASCore setting. While a chain runs the backend is in force, so a step which runs another inside its kernel, as a window does, resolves that one's kernel for it.

A backend which counts the keys it is handed shows that two patches of different channel spacings share one compiled chain, since nothing in `select` or `abs` depends on the spacing:

```{python}
from typing import ClassVar


class CountingStrict(Strict):
    """A Strict backend which counts the chains it would compile."""

    name = "counting_strict"
    keys: ClassVar[set] = set()

    def run_chain(self, steps, data):
        self.keys.add((data.shape, str(data.dtype), tuple(x.key for x in steps)))
        return super().run_chain(steps, data)


def lazy_ramp(spacing):
    recipe = Recipe.from_source(ArraySource.full((100, 4), 1.0))
    coords = {"time": np.arange(100), "distance": np.arange(4) * spacing}
    patch = dc.Patch(data=recipe, coords=coords, dims=("time", "distance"))
    return patch.set_backend("lazy[counting_strict]")


for spacing in (1.0, 2.0):
    lazy_ramp(spacing).select(time=(10, 90), samples=True).abs().load()
print(len(CountingStrict.keys))
```

## Where it happens

[`kernel_for`](`dascore.core.processor.PatchProcessor.kernel_for`) answers the lazy backend with a class's own registered lazy kernel, or else with [`lazy_kernel`](`dascore.lazy.kernels.lazy_kernel`), for the first class in the MRO which computes, whether by a kernel it writes or one registered on it; a class with none stays metadata-only. The generic kernel asks for the contract only when it describes the kernel which runs -- the class stating it is the class owning that kernel, or a subclass of it -- and refuses an operation which overrides `reconcile`, which would be handed the lazy array. For any contract but `Unchanged` it then appends a pending node, recording the contract on it. `PatchProcessor` settles that node with the output shape, dtype and `data_id` once the result's attrs are final and before the patch is built.

## Why not dask

Dask plans its work as a graph holding a task for every chunk of every operation. For very large arrays, building and scheduling that graph costs more than the work it describes. A chain holds one node for each operation, whatever the size of the array, and how the work is split into boxes is decided only when it runs.

A dask array is still accepted as a patch's data, as any other array backend is, and its dispatch is unchanged: an operation runs on dask where its kernel can, and otherwise falls back to NumPy with a warning; a patch operation run in the windows of a [`Patch.window`](`dascore.Patch.window`) is the exception, computed a piece at a time from the windows which overlap each piece, and so is one run in a [`Patch.impulse_window`](`dascore.Patch.impulse_window`), computed a chunk at a time with its measured reach around it; a reduction there still falls back, and `apply` gives back NumPy data. None of the rules above hold for it. `Patch.load` reads a dask-backed patch into memory as well, and [`Spool.io.to_xarray`](`dascore.xarray.spool.spool_to_xarray`) builds dask arrays because that is how xarray defers a read. For data larger than memory within DASCore, the lazy backend is the one to use.
